content: To effectively address snakebite envenoming and achieve sustainable change, it is essential to raise awareness among all stakeholders through broad advocacy efforts. Advocacy and communication initiatives can lead to measurable outcomes, such as resource allocation and the initiation of projects in affected countries. Over time, a strong coalition of countries, development partners, and stakeholders will be established and expanded. These efforts will be culturally and contextually tailored, delivered by local champions, advocacy groups, and activists. A standardized toolkit will be developed to provide partners with effective communication, training, and learning solutions. This will ensure that core messages are consistent across communities and countries. Tools and information resources will be prepared with adaptable core messages for different contexts. Networks of local partners will be empowered to engage with communities, and the success of these efforts will be measured by improvements in the use of prevention and risk-mitigation strategies. Effective communication and engagement regarding snakebite envenoming will leverage various media platforms, communication outlets, and stakeholders from industries, businesses, and government agencies that serve at-risk populations. Providing health promotion information to communities about snakebite envenoming can enhance the effectiveness of campaigns and related activities. Victims of snakebites are often young, healthy, and productive members of their communities until they are bitten. A comprehensive communication strategy will be developed, including core media materials and resources, to address this issue. Regional health promotion activities will be conducted in collaboration with countries, focusing on high-risk communities. Active engagement with member states and stakeholders is critical for implementing the strategy and encouraging its adoption in other countries. Increased dialogue between WHO regional and country offices, member states, and focal points will elevate the profile of snakebite envenoming and advance strategic activities. Member states should allocate resources to support the implementation of the strategy by WHO, ensuring integration, coordination, and cooperation. WHO will align its snakebite envenoming prevention and control program with its General Programme of Work and relevant regional and country health systems to maximize impact. One of the expected outcomes is an increase in the number of WHO programs incorporating snakebite envenoming activities. WHO will identify synergies with other public health programs and leverage partnerships to address the overall health needs of affected communities. Multifocal partnerships will be formed to deliver coordinated solutions, identify synergies between human and animal health programs, and provide technical support for integrating snakebite envenoming into existing health programs. Measurable outcomes will include increased international collaboration and cooperation among countries and development partners, as well as productive partnerships between WHO and other public health initiatives. Regional partnerships and alliances will be strengthened, particularly in regions with similar antivenom requirements and health system challenges. WHO will work with countries to address common issues, such as antivenom shortages, supply chain problems, and quality concerns, by establishing regional cooperation projects and creating antivenom stockpiles. Regional technical assistance and training programs will improve snakebite envenoming prevention and control, reducing morbidity, disability, and mortality. Bilateral and multinational projects will further promote the strategy's objectives. WHO will coordinate data management and analysis through the Global Health Observatory, establishing a central repository for snakebite envenoming data that is accessible to all interested parties. This will enable evidence-based decision-making and ensure that essential data are captured, analyzed, and stored in accessible repositories. Standardized national, regional, and global data on snakebite envenoming will be deposited in the Global Health Observatory, with regular data analyses published to inform decision-making. The 11th edition of the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-11) will provide global health information, including clinical and epidemiological parameters, to better understand the etiology and outcomes of snakebite envenoming. A strong investment case will be prepared to secure adequate resources for the program, based on robust data and cost-benefit analyses. Research funding will be sought to improve antivenom production technologies and products. Funding agencies should commit to increasing support for snakebite envenoming research and delivering solutions to specific problems, such as modernizing antivenom production. WHO will prepare a framework for planning, monitoring, and evaluating the strategy over time. Monitoring and evaluation will be integrated into national plans, with baseline data collected to measure progress. Progress will be regularly assessed, and annual reports will be made publicly available. For each strategic objective, pathways of change will be prioritized for short-, medium-, and long-term outcomes. The planning, monitoring, and evaluation framework will be updated throughout the program, incorporating general elements and context-specific components. WHO will prepare outcome-based work plans using a SMART approach (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) to achieve desired outcomes. Risks will be managed through a risk mitigation matrix, and resources will be identified and secured. A monitoring framework with indicators for each outcome will track progress using various data sources and verification methods. WHO will evaluate progress toward objectives and outcome targets, with particular attention to relevant indicators of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) and WHO's General Programme of Work. Evaluations will be conducted at the end of each strategy phase to assess achievements at national, regional, and global levels. WHO will develop an adaptable template for the theory of change to enhance strategy implementation, aligning context and assumptions with a logic model for mapping steps, actions, or milestones. Collaboration with countries and partners will define baseline data requirements and processes for acquiring and analyzing information. Data on incidence, morbidity, disability, and mortality will be collected for geographically defined areas, along with data on antivenoms, community prevention, healthcare-seeking behavior, and sociocultural perceptions. WHO will use a robust risk mitigation model to identify and assess risks, ensuring that the strategy is implemented effectively and sustainably.
